claim: Cerebrospinal fluid-contacting (CSF-c) neurons line the central canal of the spinal cord.
source: Cerebrospinal fluid-contacting (CSF-c) neurons line the central canal of the spinal cord and a subtype of CSF-c neurons expressing somatostatin, forms a homeostatic pH regulating system.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the anatomical location of CSF-c neurons.

claim: A subtype of CSF-c neurons expressing somatostatin forms a homeostatic pH regulating system.
source: Cerebrospinal fluid-contacting (CSF-c) neurons line the central canal of the spinal cord and a subtype of CSF-c neurons expressing somatostatin, forms a homeostatic pH regulating system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding about somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons.

claim: The density of somatostatin-containing dense-core vesicles was markedly reduced upon exposure to either alkaline or acidic pH.
source: The density of somatostatin-containing dense-core vesicles, resolved by stimulated emission depletion microscopy, was shown to be markedly reduced upon each exposure to either alkaline or acidic pH and being part of a homeostatic response inhibiting movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by STED microscopy data presented in the manuscript showing vesicle density changes.

claim: Somatostatin CSF-c neurons are part of a homeostatic response inhibiting movements.
source: The density of somatostatin-containing dense-core vesicles, resolved by stimulated emission depletion microscopy, was shown to be markedly reduced upon each exposure to either alkaline or acidic pH and being part of a homeostatic response inhibiting movements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data on pH responses.

claim: Somatostatin CSF-c neurons have sensory cilia with 9 + 0 microtubule duplets.
source: Their cilia symmetry was unravelled by stimulated emission depletion microscopy in expanded tissues as sensory with 9 + 0 microtubule duplets.
evidence: This is supported by ExSTED microscopy data showing the microtubule arrangement in cilia.

claim: Dopaminergic CSF-c neurons have a motile cilium with 9 + 2 duplets.
source: The dopaminergic CSF-c neurons on the other hand have a motile cilium with the characteristic 9 + 2 duplets and are insensitive to pH changes.
evidence: This is supported by ExSTED microscopy data showing the microtubule arrangement in dopaminergic CSF-c neuron cilia.

claim: Dopaminergic CSF-c neurons are insensitive to pH changes.
source: The dopaminergic CSF-c neurons on the other hand have a motile cilium with the characteristic 9 + 2 duplets and are insensitive to pH changes.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings and vesicle density measurements at different pH levels.

claim: The vertebrate spinal cord contains neurons with many different functions.
source: The vertebrate spinal cord contains neurons with many different functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about spinal cord organization based on established knowledge.

claim: The central canal contains cerebrospinal fluid.
source: In the middle, there is the central canal containing cerebrospinal fluid.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about the central canal.

claim: The wall of the central canal is lined with ciliated cerebrospinal fluid-contacting (CSF-c) cells in all vertebrates.
source: The wall of the central canal is lined with ciliated cerebrospinal fluid-contacting (CSF-c) cells in all vertebrates (Agduhr, 1922; Vigh et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the lamprey, many CSF-c neurons are GABAergic sometimes with co-transmitters as somatostatin, neurotensin or dopamine.
source: In the lamprey, many CSF-c neurons are GABAergic sometimes with co-transmitters as somatostatin, neurotensin or dopamine (Christenson et al., 1991; Dale et al., 1997; Jalalvand et al., 2014; Rodicio et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: CSF-c neurons located at the lateral aspect of the central canal wall coexpress somatostatin and GABA.
source: CSF-c neurons located at the lateral aspect of the central canal wall coexpress somatostatin and GABA and send axonal processes to mechanosensitive edge cells on the lateral margin of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding about the neurochemical identity of lateral CSF-c neurons.

claim: Somatostatin/GABA CSF-c neurons send axonal processes to mechanosensitive edge cells on the lateral margin of the spinal cord.
source: CSF-c neurons located at the lateral aspect of the central canal wall coexpress somatostatin and GABA and send axonal processes to mechanosensitive edge cells on the lateral margin of the spinal cord.
evidence: This describes the anatomical connectivity of these neurons.

claim: GABA/somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons act as pH and mechanosensors.
source: GABA/somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons have recently been demonstrated to act as pH and mechanosensors and be part of a pH homeostatic system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: At any deviation from neutral pH, GABA/somatostatin CSF-c neuron activity is increased, which leads to a depression of motor activity.
source: At any deviation from neutral pH their activity is increased, which in turn leads to a depression of motor activity (Jalalvand et al., 2016a; Jalalvand et al., 2016b), which should counteract the processes that have led to the pH deviation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing pH-dependent activity changes.

claim: The effect of lowering the pH on somatostatin/GABA CSF-c neurons is blocked by APETx2, a specific acid-sensing ion channel 3 (ASIC3) antagonist.
source: The effect of lowering the pH is blocked by APETx2, a specific acid-sensing ion channel 3 (ASIC3) antagonist (Diochot et al., 2004), as is their mechanosensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments and citation.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of somatostatin/GABA CSF-c neurons is blocked by APETx2.
source: The effect of lowering the pH is blocked by APETx2, a specific acid-sensing ion channel 3 (ASIC3) antagonist (Diochot et al., 2004), as is their mechanosensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments.

claim: The mechanism by which GABA/somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons cause a reduction of locomotion has been suggested to be through release of somatostatin.
source: The mechanism by which the GABA/somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons cause a reduction of locomotion has been suggested to be through release of somatostatin, since the effect on motor activity is blocked by somatostatin antagonists (Jalalvand et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments with somatostatin antagonists.

claim: CSF-c cells in a more ventral location contain dopamine.
source: CSF-c cells in a more ventral location contain dopamine (Brodin et al., 1990; Schotland et al., 1996) and their function is yet unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The function of dopamine-containing CSF-c cells is yet unknown.
source: CSF-c cells in a more ventral location contain dopamine (Brodin et al., 1990; Schotland et al., 1996) and their function is yet unknown.
evidence: This statement indicates a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Expansion microscopy allows imaging of large volumes of spinal cord tissue with single-cell resolution.
source: The physical expansion of the sample allows imaging of large volumes of spinal cord tissue with single-cell resolution and access to fine spatial information.
evidence: This describes the capability of the expansion microscopy technique used in the study.

claim: STED microscopy reaches a spatial resolution of ~40 nm.
source: STED microscopy (Hell and Wichmann, 1994; Willig et al., 2006) reaches a spatial resolution of ~40 nm, which allows us to resolve single synaptic vesicles even when the organelles are densely packed.
evidence: This describes the resolution capability of STED microscopy based on cited literature.

claim: STED microscopy allows resolution of single synaptic vesicles even when the organelles are densely packed.
source: STED microscopy (Hell and Wichmann, 1994; Willig et al., 2006) reaches a spatial resolution of ~40 nm, which allows us to resolve single synaptic vesicles even when the organelles are densely packed.
evidence: This describes the application of STED microscopy to resolve vesicles in the study.

claim: ExSTED imaging features an effective lateral spatial resolution of <10 nm.
source: ExSTED imaging features an effective lateral spatial resolution of <10 nm, and allowed us to obtain cell-type-specific structural insight, previously accessible only with electron microscopy, on the cilia subtypes in ciliated somatostatin- and dopamine-expressing CSF-c.
evidence: This describes the resolution capability of the ExSTED technique used in the study.

claim: ExSTED allows obtaining cell-type-specific structural insight on cilia subtypes that was previously accessible only with electron microscopy.
source: ExSTED imaging features an effective lateral spatial resolution of <10 nm, and allowed us to obtain cell-type-specific structural insight, previously accessible only with electron microscopy, on the cilia subtypes in ciliated somatostatin- and dopamine-expressing CSF-c.
evidence: This describes the capability of ExSTED to provide ultrastructural information.

claim: Primary (sensory) cilia have 9 + 0 microtubule duplets.
source: The cilia symmetry differs between primary (sensory) cilia (9 + 0 microtubule duplets) and motile cilia (9 + 2 microtubule duplets) and could be investigated in the context of specific cell types thanks to the spatial and specificity abilities of ExSTED.
evidence: This is a well-established structural characteristic of primary cilia.

claim: Motile cilia have 9 + 2 microtubule duplets.
source: The cilia symmetry differs between primary (sensory) cilia (9 + 0 microtubule duplets) and motile cilia (9 + 2 microtubule duplets) and could be investigated in the context of specific cell types thanks to the spatial and specificity abilities of ExSTED.
evidence: This is a well-established structural characteristic of motile cilia.

claim: Dopamine CSF-c neurons have motile cilia that may contribute to the flow of the cerebrospinal fluid.
source: We could show that dopamine CSF-c neurons have motile cilia that may contribute to the flow of the cerebrospinal fluid, whereas somatostatin CSF-c neurons instead have predominantly sensory cilia conveying pH and mechanosensitivity.
evidence: This is based on the structural characterization of cilia in dopamine CSF-c neurons and inference about their function.

claim: Somatostatin CSF-c neurons have predominantly sensory cilia conveying pH and mechanosensitivity.
source: We could show that dopamine CSF-c neurons have motile cilia that may contribute to the flow of the cerebrospinal fluid, whereas somatostatin CSF-c neurons instead have predominantly sensory cilia conveying pH and mechanosensitivity.
evidence: This is based on the structural characterization of cilia and functional properties of somatostatin CSF-c neurons.

claim: The final expansion factor of the expansion microscopy protocol was about ~4.5.
source: An experimental design for expanding and handling spinal cord tissue was developed, which includes slicing, fluorescent immunolabelling of somatostatin and dopaminergic CFS-c neurons in 80–100 µm thick spinal cord slices, and the expansion steps with a final expansion factor of about ~4.5 (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: ExLSM enables recording a volume of 360 × 250 × 200 µm³ containing a large population of CSF-c neurons where individual cells can be recognized and counted.
source: The combination of our spinal cord expansion protocol and light-sheet microscopy (ExLSM) enables us to record a volume of 360  ×  250  ×  200  µm3 containing a large population of CSF-c neurons where the individual cells can be recognized and counted (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This describes the imaging capability demonstrated in the study with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons are found throughout the whole volume and located laterally relative to the central canal.
source: Somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons are found throughout the whole volume and located laterally relative to the central canal, while the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons are located ventrally, confirming that the observation on individual sections is maintained in large volume with a high degree of order.
evidence: This is based on ExLSM imaging data showing the spatial distribution of these neurons.

claim: Dopaminergic CSF-c neurons are located ventrally.
source: Somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons are found throughout the whole volume and located laterally relative to the central canal, while the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons are located ventrally, confirming that the observation on individual sections is maintained in large volume with a high degree of order.
evidence: This is based on ExLSM imaging data showing the spatial distribution of these neurons.

claim: There is a higher amount of somatostatin CSF-c neurons compared to dopaminergic CSF-c neurons in all four areas of the spinal cord examined.
source: We quantified the distribution of CSF-c neuronal subtypes at four different levels of the spinal cord, resulting in a higher amount of somatostatin CSF-c neurons compared to the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons in all four areas of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cells from ExLSM data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In a specific position (area 2) the somatostatin CSF-c neurons were more abundant than in other parts.
source: Additionally, in a specific position (area 2) the somatostatin CSF-c neurons were more abundant than in other parts (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Somatostatin and dopamine are stored in dense-core vesicles (DCVs).
source: Somatostatin and dopamine are stored in dense-core vesicles (DCVs) and were found in the soma, bulb protrusion (Figure 2A–C,E–G), and projections (data not shown) of the CSF-c neurons.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and STED imaging shown in Figure 2.

claim: Somatostatin and dopamine DCVs were found in the soma, bulb protrusion, and projections of the CSF-c neurons.
source: Somatostatin and dopamine are stored in dense-core vesicles (DCVs) and were found in the soma, bulb protrusion (Figure 2A–C,E–G), and projections (data not shown) of the CSF-c neurons.
evidence: This describes the subcellular localization of DCVs based on imaging data.

claim: The average diameter of somatostatin and dopamine DCVs was 100–120 nm with vesicles as small as 60 nm (FWHM) measured with STED.
source: In both cases, the average diameter of somatostatin and dopamine DCVs was 100–120 nm with vesicles as small as 60 nm (full width at half maximum, FWHM; Figure 2D, H) measured with STED.
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy measurements shown in Figure 2D and H.

claim: Using confocal microscopy resulted in an overestimation of vesicle size with 250–300 nm (FWHM).
source: However, using confocal microscopy, resulted in an overestimation of vesicle size with 250–300 nm (FWHM; Figure 2D, H).
evidence: This is based on comparison of confocal and STED measurements shown in Figure 2D and H.

claim: The data on somatostatin and dopamine DCVs diameter recorded with STED are compatible with previously published electron microscopy data.
source: Our data on the somatostatin and dopamine DCVs diameter recorded with STED are compatible with previously published electron microscopy data (Schotland et al., 1996).
evidence: This compares the current STED measurements with previous EM data from the literature.

claim: The somatostatin CSF-c neurons in the lamprey spinal cord also express GABA.
source: The somatostatin CSF-c neurons in the lamprey spinal cord also express GABA (Brodin et al., 1990; Christenson et al., 1991; Jalalvand et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Somatostatin/GABA CSF-c neurons are sensitive to pH changes of the cerebrospinal fluid.
source: We have recently shown that somatostatin/GABA CSF-c neurons are sensitive to pH changes of the cerebrospinal fluid (Jalalvand et al., 2016a; Jalalvand et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies by the authors.

claim: The number density of somatostatin DCVs measured for the soma of CSF-c neurons decreased markedly in either acidic or alkaline pH conditions.
source: The number density of somatostatin DCVs measured for the soma of CSF-c neurons both in areas (Figure 3G) and volumes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) decreased markedly in CSF-c neurons in either acidic or alkaline pH conditions.
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy quantification shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Slices stained with a GABA antibody did not show any changes in fluorescence intensity at different pH.
source: In contrast, the slices stained with a GABA antibody did not show any changes in fluorescence intensity at different pH (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 3H-K.

claim: STED images of somatostatin DCVs and GABA-expressing CSF-c neurons did not show colocalization of somatostatin DCVs and GABA in the soma.
source: STED images of somatostatin DCVs and GABA-expressing CSF-c neurons did not show colocalization of somatostatin DCVs and GABA in the soma (Figure 3M–O).
evidence: This is based on dual-color STED imaging shown in Figure 3M-O.

claim: The GABA signal was not significantly different when measured in or outside of somatostatin DCVs, neither in the soma nor in the axons.
source: The GABA signal was not significantly different when measured in or outside of somatostatin DCVs, neither in the soma nor in the axons (Figure 3P).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of GABA signal shown in Figure 3P.

claim: There is no correlation between GABA and somatostatin signals in somatostatin vesicles.
source: The results confirmed that there is no correlation between GABA and somatostatin signals in somatostatin vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the imaging data analysis.

claim: During pH changes of the extracellular solution vesicles containing somatostatin are released, resulting in fewer DCVs in the soma, while GABA is not co-released.
source: Our imaging data support the conclusion that during pH changes of the extracellular solution vesicles containing somatostatin are released, resulting in fewer DCVs in the soma, while GABA is not co-released.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined imaging data showing differential release of somatostatin and GABA.

claim: There was no significant change in the number density of dopaminergic DCVs after perfusion with acidic or alkaline pH solutions, neither in cell areas nor in cell volumes.
source: The result showed no significant change in the number density of dopaminergic DCVs after perfusion with acidic or alkaline pH solutions, neither in cell areas (Figure 4D) nor in cell volumes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy quantification shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All recorded dopaminergic CSF-c neurons fired spontaneous action potentials, depolarizing synaptic potentials, and hyperpolarizing synaptic potentials.
source: All recorded dopaminergic CSF-c neurons fired spontaneous action potentials, depolarizing synaptic potentials, and hyperpolarizing synaptic potentials (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: During bath-applied extracellular solutions of acidic pH (6.5) or alkaline pH (8.5) no changes in spike frequency were observed in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons, nor a net depolarization of the resting membrane potential.
source: During bath-applied extracellular solutions of acidic pH (6.5) or alkaline pH (8.5) no changes in spike frequency were observed, nor a net depolarization of the resting membrane potential (Figure 4E1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In contrast to the somatostatin CSF-c neurons the dopamine CSF-c are not sensitive to pH changes.
source: Thus, in contrast to the somatostatin CSF-c neurons the dopamine CSF-c are not sensitive to pH changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological and imaging data comparing the two cell types.

claim: All neurons labelled with Neurobiotin during the patch-clamp recording were tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunoreactive.
source: All neurons labelled with Neurobiotin during the patch-clamp recording were tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunoreactive (Figure 4F, H).
evidence: This confirms the identity of recorded neurons through post-hoc immunostaining shown in Figure 4F and H.

claim: Both somatostatin and dopamine CSF-c neurons are ciliated.
source: Both somatostatin and dopamine CSF-c neurons are ciliated (see below) and the former known to be mechanosensitive (Jalalvand et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data and citations.

claim: Somatostatin CSF-c neurons are known to be mechanosensitive.
source: Both somatostatin and dopamine CSF-c neurons are ciliated (see below) and the former known to be mechanosensitive (Jalalvand et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Dopamine CSF-c neurons responded with an action potential and a distinct mechanosensitive response to brief fluid pulses applied near their bulb protrusion.
source: Dopamine CSF-c neurons responded with an action potential and a distinct mechanosensitive response (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In the presence of APETx2 dopamine CSF-c neurons still observed a mechanosensitive response.
source: In the presence of APETx2 we still observed a mechanosensitive response (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings with APETx2 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of dopamine CSF-c neurons is not mediated by ASIC3.
source: Thus, the mechanosensitivity is not mediated by ASIC3 in dopamine CSF-c neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the APETx2 experiment showing no blockade of mechanosensitivity.

claim: In situ hybridization showed expression of polycystic kidney disease 2-like 1 (PKD2L1) channels in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons.
source: In situ hybridization showed expression of polycystic kidney disease 2-like 1 (PKD2L1) channels in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: PKD2L1 has been confirmed as a mechanosensitive ion channel in zebrafish.
source: As PKD2L1 has been confirmed as a mechanosensitive ion channel in zebrafish (Böhm et al., 2016; Sternberg et al., 2018), the results suggest that the mechanosensitivity of the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons may be mediated by PKD2L1 channels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in zebrafish.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons may be mediated by PKD2L1 channels.
source: As PKD2L1 has been confirmed as a mechanosensitive ion channel in zebrafish (Böhm et al., 2016; Sternberg et al., 2018), the results suggest that the mechanosensitivity of the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons may be mediated by PKD2L1 channels.
evidence: This is a speculation based on PKD2L1 expression in dopamine CSF-c neurons and its known function in zebrafish.

claim: The mechanical response of somatostatin CSF-c neurons is blocked by an ASIC3 antagonist.
source: In contrast, the mechanical response of somatostatin CSF-c neurons is blocked by an ASIC3 antagonist.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to dopamine CSF-c neurons and is supported by previous studies.

claim: Dopamine CSF-c neurons are not sensing pH changes as their somatostatin counterparts, but both are mechanosensitive.
source: In conclusion, dopamine CSF-c neurons are not sensing pH changes as their somatostatin counterparts, but both are mechanosensitive.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The mechanical transduction is blocked by an ASIC3 antagonist in somatostatin CSF-c neurons and may be mediated by PKD2L1 in the dopamine CSF-c neurons as in the zebrafish.
source: The mechanical transduction is blocked by an ASIC3 antagonist in somatostatin CSF-c neurons and may be mediated by PKD2L1 in the dopamine CSF-c neurons as in the zebrafish.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the pharmacological and molecular data.

claim: Cilia express acetylated α-tubulin.
source: Cilia express acetylated α-tubulin and can be classified either as primary cilia, mainly present in sensory cells and neurons and with a 9 + 0 symmetry of nine outer microtubule doublets, or motile cilia, with a 9 + 2 symmetry showing an extra pair of microtubule singlets in the centre (Gaertig and Wloga, 2008; Satir, 2005).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of cilia supported by citations.

claim: Primary cilia are mainly present in sensory cells and neurons.
source: Cilia express acetylated α-tubulin and can be classified either as primary cilia, mainly present in sensory cells and neurons and with a 9 + 0 symmetry of nine outer microtubule doublets, or motile cilia, with a 9 + 2 symmetry showing an extra pair of microtubule singlets in the centre (Gaertig and Wloga, 2008; Satir, 2005).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of primary cilia supported by citations.

claim: Primary and motile cilia both have an average diameter of 200–240 nm.
source: Primary and motile cilia both have an average diameter of 200–240 nm, close to the achievable spatial resolution of a confocal microscope equipped with a high numerical aperture objective.
evidence: This is a statement about the size of cilia based on known structural information.

claim: STED imaging visualizes the cilium as a hollow structure with an outer diameter of about 240 nm.
source: STED imaging visualizes the cilium as a hollow structure with an outer diameter of about 240 nm thanks to the increased spatial resolution, but the resolution is still not enough to detect the microtubule doublets.
evidence: This is based on STED imaging data of cilia.

claim: STED resolution is still not enough to detect the microtubule doublets in cilia.
source: STED imaging visualizes the cilium as a hollow structure with an outer diameter of about 240 nm thanks to the increased spatial resolution, but the resolution is still not enough to detect the microtubule doublets.
evidence: This explains the limitation of STED for resolving internal ciliary structure.

claim: Confocal imaging of the expanded sample shows spatial details comparable to STED images of the non-expanded one.
source: Confocal imaging of the expanded sample shows spatial details comparable to STED images (Figure 5C) of the non-expanded one, therefore still not having the resolution (5–10 nm) needed to dissect the internal cilia structure and identify microtubule doublets.
evidence: This is based on comparison of imaging modalities shown in Figure 5.

claim: By using the combination of STED microscopy and expanded tissue (ExSTED), it was possible to add a factor of ~four to five to the typical 50 nm resolution of STED microscopy and therefore resolving at the smaller spatial scale of 5–10 nm.
source: By using the combination of STED microscopy and expanded tissue (ExSTED), we were able to add a factor of ~four to five to the typical 50 nm resolution of STED microscopy and therefore resolving at the smaller spatial scale of 5–10 nm (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the resolution enhancement achieved by ExSTED shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: ExSTED made it possible to separate high-density cilia within the 3D geometry of the central canal.
source: In this way, it was possible to separate high-density cilia within the 3D geometry of the central canal (Figure 5—video 1) due to the increased imaging resolution and further resolve their internal structure and allowing to classify them as motile or sensory (Figure 5D).
evidence: This describes the capability of ExSTED demonstrated in the study.

claim: In some cilia, the central pair of tubules was clearly observed with a peak-to-peak distance of 70 nm.
source: In some cilia, the central pair of tubules was clearly observed with a peak-to-peak distance of 70 nm (Figure 5P–R).
evidence: This is based on ExSTED imaging measurements shown in Figure 5P-R.

claim: Both types of cilia symmetries in the lamprey spinal cord were explored: sensory and motile cilia symmetries.
source: Both types of cilia symmetries in the lamprey spinal cord were explored: sensory (Figure 5I–M) and motile cilia symmetries (Figure 5N–R).
evidence: This is based on ExSTED imaging shown in Figure 5I-M and 5N-R.

claim: The presence of motile cilia in the central canal of the lamprey has been shown with electron microscopy.
source: The presence of motile cilia in the central canal of the lamprey has been shown with electron microscopy (Schotland et al., 1996; Vigh et al., 2004), but with ExSTED we could detect both motile and sensory cilia symmetries in this area.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous EM studies.

claim: With ExSTED both motile and sensory cilia symmetries could be detected in the central canal area.
source: The presence of motile cilia in the central canal of the lamprey has been shown with electron microscopy (Schotland et al., 1996; Vigh et al., 2004), but with ExSTED we could detect both motile and sensory cilia symmetries in this area.
evidence: This describes the new finding enabled by ExSTED.

claim: Of 70 cilia belonging to somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons, 60 cilia were primary (9 + 0 symmetry) and 10 cilia were motile (9 + 2 symmetry).
source: In our data, 70 cilia belong to somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons (n = 70). Of these, 60 cilia were primary (9 + 0 symmetry) and 10 cilia were motile (9 + 2 symmetry) (Figure 6D–K, T).
evidence: This is based on ExSTED imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6D-K and T.

claim: 20 cilia of dopaminergic CSF-c neurons were all motile cilia (9 + 2 symmetry).
source: Additionally, 20 cilia of dopaminergic CSF-c neurons were all motile cilia (9 + 2 symmetry) (Figure 6L–S, T).
evidence: This is based on ExSTED imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6L-S and T.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons are sensory neurons expressing mainly sensory cilia.
source: We found that somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons are sensory neurons expressing mainly sensory cilia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the predominance of 9+0 cilia in these neurons.

claim: The motile cilia in both somatostatin-expressing and dopaminergic CSF-c neurons might be involved in contributing to the flow of CSF through the central canal.
source: However, the motile cilia in both somatostatin-expressing and dopaminergic CSF-c neurons might be involved in contributing to the flow of CSF through the central canal (Figure 6U).
evidence: This is a speculation about the function of motile cilia based on their structural characteristics.

claim: Expression of both ASIC3 and PKD2L1 could be detected on the cilia of spinal CSF-c neurons in mice.
source: Interestingly, we could detect the expression of both ASIC3 and PKD2L1 on the cilia of spinal CSF-c neurons in mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–Q).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data in mouse shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-Q.

claim: Arl13b, a ciliary protein, has high expression in sensory cilia.
source: Besides, we visualized Arl13b, a ciliary protein on cilia that has high expression in sensory cilia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1R–V).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1R-V and known properties of Arl13b.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing and dopaminergic CSF-c neurons mainly have one cilium, but in rare cases (N = 8) two cilia per bulb of these neurons were detected by ExM.
source: As reported, somatostatin-expressing and dopaminergic CSF-c neurons mainly have one cilium, but we could in rare cases (N = 8) detect two cilia per bulb of these neurons by ExM (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is based on ExM imaging shown in Figure 7.

claim: There were approximately twice as many somatostatin CSF-c neurons as dopaminergic CSF-c neurons along the whole length of the spinal cord.
source: There were approximately twice as many somatostatin CSF-c neurons as dopaminergic CSF-c neurons along the whole length of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantification results from ExLSM.

claim: One area, at the level of the rostral part of the dorsal fin had a somewhat larger number of somatostatin CSF-c neurons than elsewhere.
source: One area, at the level of the rostral part of the dorsal fin had, however, a somewhat larger number of somatostatin CSF-c neurons than elsewhere.
evidence: This is based on the quantification data from ExLSM.

claim: This is the same spinal cord area in which a dramatic decrease occurs of the serotonin/dopamine neurons that are located just ventral to the central canal.
source: This is the same spinal cord area in which a dramatic decrease occurs of the serotonin/dopamine neurons that are located just ventral to the central canal (Figure 8A, Schotland et al., 1995; Zhang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The size distribution of somatostatin and dopamine DCVs is in line with previous electron microscopy studies.
source: The size distribution is in line with previous electron microscopy studies (Schotland et al., 1996).
evidence: This compares the current findings with previous EM data.

claim: The STED data reveal the presence of DCVs in several CSF-c cellular subcompartments, including the bulb protrusion into the central canal, soma, and axonal branches.
source: The STED data reveal the presence of DCVs in several CSF-c cellular subcompartments, including the bulb protrusion into the central canal, soma, and axonal branches.
evidence: This is based on STED imaging data showing DCV distribution.

claim: A marked reduction of somatostatin DCVs number density in the soma of CSF-c neurons when exposed to acidic or alkaline pH was shown.
source: We could show a marked reduction of somatostatin DCVs number density in the soma of CSF-c neurons when exposed to acidic or alkaline pH, while there was no effect on the dopamine DCVs number density.
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy quantification data.

claim: There was no effect on the dopamine DCVs number density when exposed to acidic or alkaline pH.
source: We could show a marked reduction of somatostatin DCVs number density in the soma of CSF-c neurons when exposed to acidic or alkaline pH, while there was no effect on the dopamine DCVs number density.
evidence: This is based on STED microscopy quantification data.

claim: This lack of change in the number density of DCVs in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons agrees with the electrophysiological results showing that these cells are not activated by changes of the extracellular pH.
source: This lack of change in the number density of DCVs in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons agrees with the present electrophysiological results showing that these cells are not activated by changes of the extracellular pH.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the imaging and electrophysiology data.

claim: Somatostatin/GABA-expressing CSF-c neurons are responding to acidic and alkaline extracellular solutions being part of a homeostatic system for reducing motor activity when the spinal cord/brain is exposed to changes of pH.
source: We have shown previously that somatostatin/GABA-expressing CSF-c neurons are responding to acidic and alkaline extracellular solutions (Jalalvand et al., 2016a; Jalalvand et al., 2016b) being part of a homeostatic system for reducing motor activity when the spinal cord/brain is exposed to changes of pH as due to metabolic or respiratory stress or intense muscle activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: The pH response of somatostatin/GABA CSF-c neurons resulted from somatostatin DCVs release, whereas GABA was unaffected.
source: We now show with STED imaging that the pH response resulted from somatostatin DCVs release, whereas GABA was unaffected.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the STED imaging data showing differential release.

claim: GABAergic CSF-c neurons have been shown to have ciliated endings in the lamprey and other species at the ultrastructural level.
source: At the ultrastructural level, GABAergic CSF-c neurons have been shown to have ciliated endings in the lamprey and other species (Orts-Del'Immagine et al., 2014; Schotland et al., 1996; Vigh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous ultrastructural studies.

claim: ExSTED microscopy allowed obtaining cell-type-specific structural insights on the cilium types in ciliated somatostatin- and dopamine-expressing CSF-c neurons.
source: ExSTED microscopy allowed us to obtain cell-type-specific structural insights on the cilium types in ciliated somatostatin- and dopamine-expressing CSF-c neurons, respectively (Figure 8B).
evidence: This summarizes the capability of ExSTED demonstrated in the study.

claim: Using ExSTED microscopy primary cilia with 9 + 0 symmetry were found in somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons.
source: Using ExSTED microscopy we found primary cilia with 9 + 0 symmetry in somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons, also found in specialized sensory cells (Kirschen and Xiong, 2017; Singla and Reiter, 2006) and motile cilia with 9 + 2 symmetry in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons that may serve to generate fluid flow (Faubel et al., 2016; Satir and Christensen, 2007).
evidence: This is based on ExSTED imaging data and supported by citations about sensory cilia.

claim: Motile cilia with 9 + 2 symmetry were found in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons that may serve to generate fluid flow.
source: Using ExSTED microscopy we found primary cilia with 9 + 0 symmetry in somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons, also found in specialized sensory cells (Kirschen and Xiong, 2017; Singla and Reiter, 2006) and motile cilia with 9 + 2 symmetry in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons that may serve to generate fluid flow (Faubel et al., 2016; Satir and Christensen, 2007).
evidence: This is based on ExSTED imaging data and supported by citations about motile cilia function.

claim: The high expression of sensory cilia (9 + 0) found in pH/mechanosensitive somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons provide additional evidence to recognize them as sensory neurons.
source: The high expression of sensory cilia (9 + 0) found in pH/mechanosensitive somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons provide additional evidence to recognize them as sensory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural and functional properties of these neurons.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of the somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons is blocked by APETx2, a selective ASIC3 blocker.
source: The mechanosensitivity of the dopamine- and somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons is mediated by different cellular mechanisms, the latter is blocked by APETx2, a selective ASIC3 blocker as shown in previous studies (Jalalvand et al., 2016a; Jalalvand et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of the dopamine CSF-c neurons is unaffected by APETx2.
source: The mechanosensitivity of the dopamine CSF-c neurons is, however, unaffected by APETx2.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data with APETx2.

claim: APETx2 is specific to the ASIC3 but does not block ASIC1 receptors.
source: This blocker is specific to the ASIC3 but does not block ASIC1 receptors (Diochot et al., 2004), the latter having been cloned in lamprey (Coric et al., 2005) and found insensitive to pH.
evidence: This is supported by citations about APETx2 specificity and ASIC1 in lamprey.

claim: ASIC1 has been cloned in lamprey and found insensitive to pH.
source: This blocker is specific to the ASIC3 but does not block ASIC1 receptors (Diochot et al., 2004), the latter having been cloned in lamprey (Coric et al., 2005) and found insensitive to pH.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on lamprey ASIC1.

claim: The data support the interpretation that ASIC3 mediates both the acid-sensing and the mechanosensitivity in somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons.
source: The data support the previous interpretation that ASIC3 mediates both the acid-sensing and the mechanosensitivity, in somatostatin-expressing CSF-c neurons (Jalalvand et al., 2016a; Jalalvand et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current and previous data.

claim: PKD2L1 channel is expressed in the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons.
source: PKD2L1 channel is expressed in the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and this channel is known to serve as a mechanosensitive receptor (Kamura et al., 2011; Nauli et al., 2003) and may therefore serve in this function also for the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: PKD2L1 channel is known to serve as a mechanosensitive receptor.
source: PKD2L1 channel is expressed in the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and this channel is known to serve as a mechanosensitive receptor (Kamura et al., 2011; Nauli et al., 2003) and may therefore serve in this function also for the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on PKD2L1 function.

claim: PKD2L1 may serve as a mechanosensitive receptor for the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons.
source: PKD2L1 channel is expressed in the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and this channel is known to serve as a mechanosensitive receptor (Kamura et al., 2011; Nauli et al., 2003) and may therefore serve in this function also for the dopaminergic CSF-c neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on PKD2L1 expression and known function.

claim: In the zebrafish, the mechanosensitive GABA CSF-c neurons sense the lateral bending movements occurring during locomotion through PKD2L1 channels.
source: In the zebrafish, the mechanosensitive GABA CSF-c neurons sense the lateral bending movements occurring during locomotion through PKD2L1 channels (Fidelin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study in zebrafish.

claim: Expression of ASIC3 and PKD2L1 channels, as well as sensory cilia in CSF-c neurons of the mouse was observed, which suggests that this may be representative of all vertebrates.
source: We have also observed expression of ASIC3 and PKD2L1 channels, as well as sensory cilia in CSF-c neurons of the mouse, which suggests that this may be representative of all vertebrates.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data in mouse and is a speculation about conservation across vertebrates.

claim: The motile cilia (9 + 2) found only in the mechanosensitive (non-pH) dopaminergic CSF-c neurons may suggest that they may act as a CSF flow generator.
source: The motile cilia (9 + 2) found only in the mechanosensitive (non-pH) dopaminergic CSF-c neurons may suggest that they may act as a CSF flow generator.
evidence: This is a speculation about the function of motile cilia in dopaminergic CSF-c neurons.

claim: By applying ExM combined with light-sheet and STED microscopy with nanoscale precision, the spatial organization, abundance, and subcellular composition of two distinct GABAergic CSF-c neuronal subtypes in the lamprey spinal cord were elucidated.
source: In conclusion, by applying ExM combined with light-sheet and STED microscopy with nanoscale precision, the spatial organization, abundance, and subcellular composition of two distinct GABAergic CSF-c neuronal subtypes in the lamprey spinal cord were elucidated.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: One type of CSF-c neuron is sensitive to pH and displaying mechanosensitivity (somatostatin) while the other (dopamine) only responds to mechanical stimuli.
source: One type is sensitive to pH and displaying mechanosensitivity (somatostatin) while the other (dopamine) only responds to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional differences between the two CSF-c neuron types.

claim: The two CSF-c neuron types use different cellular mechanisms for the transduction of mechanical stimuli to their cilia.
source: They use different cellular mechanisms for the transduction of mechanical stimuli to their cilia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pharmacological and molecular data.

claim: Experiments were performed on a total of 40 adult river lampreys (Lampetra fluviatilis) of both sexes that were collected from the Ljusnan River, Hälsingland, Sweden.
source: Experiments were performed on a total of 40 adult river lampreys (Lampetra fluviatilis) of both sexes that were collected from the Ljusnan River, Hälsingland, Sweden.
evidence: This describes the animal subjects used in the study.

claim: Experiments were performed on a total of 4, C57BL/6 wild type mice (Mus musculus).
source: Experiments were performed on a total of 4, C57BL/6 wild type mice (Mus musculus).
evidence: This describes the mouse subjects used in the study.
